context_blurb:
Water is sticky. It beads into round drops, bears insects on a pond, climbs thin tubes and rises to the tops of the tallest trees, and its ice floats. All of it comes from one fact: the two ends of a water molecule carry slight, opposite electric charges.

A water molecule, H2O, is an oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms, each bond a pair of shared electrons. Oxygen tugs harder on those electrons and keeps them closer. Electrons carry negative charge, so the oxygen end is left slightly negative and each hydrogen end slightly positive. No electron leaves or joins, so the molecule stays neutral overall; its electrons only shift toward one end, which makes it polar, slightly charged at each end.

Opposite charges attract, so when two water molecules meet, the oxygen end of one draws a hydrogen end of the other. That pull, a hydrogen bond, is far weaker than the bonds inside a molecule and is not a shared pair of electrons, but each molecule makes several at once. Together these bonds give water its cohesion, its cling to itself.

Cohesion draws water's surface in as tight as it will go, and a ball wraps its water in less surface than any other shape. Aboard the space station, where the station and everything in it fall around Earth together, a loose blob of water does not sag under its weight, so its molecules pull it into the shape with least surface: a nearly perfect ball. The drop's own gravity is far too weak to round it; even an icy moon 420 kilometres across can stay lumpy.

Cohesion also gives water a skin. Deep down, each molecule is tugged equally on every side, so the pulls cancel. A molecule at the top has water only beside and below it and almost nothing pulling from the air above, so the surface molecules are pulled inward by the water around and below them. The top layer draws tight: surface tension, which lets a water strider dimple a pond without sinking.

That skin can bear a steel paper clip set down gently, though steel is nearly eight times denser (heavier for its size) than water. A soap molecule has one end drawn to water and one end that is not, so soap crowds into the surface with those other ends poking into the air. There it weakens the pull of the surface molecules on each other, cutting their grip to less than half, and the clip sinks.

Water also clings to other things: adhesion. Water clings to glass more than to itself, so in a narrow glass tube it creeps up the wall, its surface curving up at the edges, and draws a column up above the level outside. Mercury, a liquid metal, clings to itself far more than to glass, so in a tube dipped in mercury the surface bulges and is held down below the level outside.

In 1718 the English doctor James Jurin showed the Royal Society how water rises in glass tubes of different widths. The narrower the tube, the higher the water climbed: half as wide, twice as high, and a tube 0.4 millimetres across lifts water about 7 centimetres. The glass pulls the water up all round the edge of its surface, and a narrow tube has less water to hold up for each bit of edge. Francis Hauksbee had already shown that the glass's thickness makes no difference.

In 1894 John Joly and Henry Dixon explained how cohesion and adhesion lift water up a coast redwood, over 100 metres, and their explanation is still the leading one. As water evaporates from the leaves, it tugs on the water behind it in the wood's thin tubes. Since water clings to itself and to the tube walls, the tug passes down an unbroken thread to the roots: evaporation at the leaves pulls up a clinging chain of water. Eduard Strasburger found water still rising in plants whose living cells had been poisoned, so no living pump is needed.

Hydrogen bonds even explain floating ice. As water freezes, each molecule's charged ends lock onto exactly four neighbours, building an open, six-sided pattern with empty gaps. In the liquid the molecules tumble closer together, but in ice they lock into an open pattern, held farther apart, so water swells by about nine percent as it freezes, and the ice, less dense than the water, floats. The molecules themselves stay the same size.
